We had two delays that month and the team spent all its energy on the wrong one. The first was the architectural package, which slipped by three weeks. Everybody panicked, because three weeks sounds bad. But that package had five weeks of float, it fed nothing urgent, and if it had slipped by four weeks the end date still would not have moved. The second delay was four days on a set of connection details, and almost nobody noticed it. Those four days were on the critical path, feeding an order with a fourteen-week lead time, and four days there were four days on the whole project. So now, before I let anybody discuss a delay, I ask one question. Is it on the critical path, yes or no. If the answer is no, we write it down and we move on. If the answer is yes, then we stop everything and talk about it properly, even if it is one day.

The hardest call is the one where you know the date has moved and you do not yet have the recovery plan. Most people wait, because they want to arrive with a solution. I understand that instinct and I think it is wrong. Every week you wait, the client loses a week of their own options, and they will work that out afterwards. What I do instead is call early and say three things. This has moved, by this much. This is what it hits. And I do not have the recovery plan yet, I will have it on Thursday. Clients take that much better than people expect, because it is the only version that lets them do something. What they ask, almost always, is the same three questions. Is it going to move again. What would have to happen for the original date to hold. And what would you do if it were your money. That third one is the one to prepare, because if you have not thought about it, everything else you said sounds rehearsed.
